plain_english:
Aren't you ashamed of being more cowardly and pathetic than runaway slaves? When they escape, how do they leave their masters? What property do they count on? What servants help them? They steal just a little bit — enough for a few days — then they figure out how to survive as they go. They cross land and sea. They come up with one plan after another to stay alive. Has any runaway slave ever starved to death? But you're terrified that you won't have what you need. You lose sleep over it. You fool, are you so blind that you can't see where this fear of lacking necessities leads? Where does it lead? To the same place that fever leads, or a falling stone — to death. Haven't you said this to your friends countless times? Haven't you read and written about this very thing? How often have you bragged that you were comfortable with death?

So learn first what things are truly shameful. Then come tell us you're a philosopher. But right now, don't claim that title — not even if someone else calls you one.
original_excerpt:
Are you not ashamed at being more cowardly and more mean than fugitive slaves? How do they when they run away leave their masters? on what estates do they depend, and what domestics do they rely on? Do they not after stealing a little, which is enough for the first days, then afterwards move on through land or through sea, contriving one method after another for maintaining their lives? And what fugitive slave ever died of hunger? But you are afraid lest necessary things should fail you, and are sleepless by night. Wretch, are you so blind, and don't you see the road to which the want of necessaries leads?—Well, where does it lead?—to the same place to which a fever leads, or a stone that falls on you, to death. Have you not often said this yourself to your companions? have you not read much of this kind, and written much? and how often have you boasted that you were easy as to death?

Learn then first what are the things which are shameful, and then tell us that you are a philosopher: but at present do not, even if any other man calls you so, allow it.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want

plain_english: Are you ashamed of things that aren't your doing? Things you didn't cause? Things that just happened to you, like a headache or fever? If your parents were poor and left their money to someone else, if they don't help you while they're alive — is that shameful for you? Is this what you learned from the philosophers? Didn't you ever hear that only shameful acts deserve blame? And only things worthy of blame should be blamed? Who do you blame for something they didn't do themselves? Did you make your father the way he is? Can you change him? Do you have that power? No. So why wish for things you can't have? Why be ashamed when you don't get them?
original_excerpt: Is that shameful to you which is not your own act, that of which you are not the cause, that which has come to you by accident, as a headache, as a fever? If your parents were poor, and left their property to others, and if while they live, they do not help you at all, is this shameful to you? Is this what you learned with the philosophers? Did you never hear that the thing which is shameful ought to be blamed, and that which is blamable is worthy of blame? Whom do you blame for an act which is not his own, which he did not do himself? Did you then make your father such as he is, or is it in your power to improve him? Is this power given to you? Well then, ought you to wish the things which are not given to you, or to be ashamed if you do not obtain them?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want

plain_english: And have you gotten used to studying philosophy while looking to other people for help? Have you learned to expect nothing from yourself? Then go ahead and complain and moan. Eat your meals in fear that you won't have food tomorrow. Shake with worry about your poor slaves — that they might steal from you, run away, or die. Live like this. Keep living like this. You who have only pretended to study philosophy. You who have made its teachings look as worthless as possible by proving they don't help anyone who tries to use them. You never looked for inner strength, peace of mind, or freedom from destructive emotions. You never sought out anyone to help you with these goals. You only looked for people who could teach you clever arguments. You never seriously asked yourself any of these key questions: Can I handle this, or can't I? What should I do next?
original_excerpt: And have you also been accustomed while you were studying philosophy to look to others and to hope for nothing from yourself? Lament then and groan and eat with fear that you may not have food to-morrow. Tremble about your poor slaves lest they steal, lest they run away, lest they die. So live, and continue to live, you who in name only have approached philosophy, and have disgraced its theorems as far as you can by showing them to be useless and unprofitable to those who take them up; you who have never sought constancy, freedom from perturbation, and from passions; you who have not sought any person for the sake of this object, but many for the sake of syllogisms; you who have never thoroughly examined any of these appearances by yourself, Am I able to bear, or am I not able to bear? What remains for me to do?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want

plain_english: But you act like everything in your life is fine and secure. So you've been focusing on the third topic — keeping things unchanged so you can hold onto what? Your cowardice, your petty spirit, your worship of rich people, your endless wanting without getting anything, and your failed attempts to avoid what you don't like? That's what you're trying to make secure.
original_excerpt: But as if all your affairs were well and secure, you have been resting on the third topic, that of things being unchanged, in order that you may possess unchanged—what? cowardice, mean spirit, the admiration of the rich, desire without attaining any end, and avoidance ([Greek: echchlisin]) which fails in the attempt? About security in these things you have been anxious.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want

plain_english: Shouldn't you have gained something extra from all your reasoning? And then protected it properly? Have you ever seen anyone build a wall around nothing? What's the point of posting a guard at a door that doesn't exist? You practice so you can prove things — but prove what exactly? You practice so sophisms won't toss you around like waves at sea. But tossed around from what secure position? First show me what you actually hold onto, what you measure, what you weigh. Show me your scales or your measuring cup. How long will you keep measuring dust? Shouldn't you be demonstrating the things that make people happy? The things that help life go the way they want? Why we shouldn't blame anyone or accuse anyone, and why we should accept how the universe works?
original_excerpt: Ought you not to have gained something in addition from reason, and then to have protected this with security? And whom did you ever see building a battlement all around and encircling it with a wall? And what doorkeeper is placed with no door to watch? But you practise in order to be able to prove—what? You practise that you may not be tossed as on the sea through sophisms, and tossed about from what? Show me first what you hold, what you measure, or what you weigh; and show me the scales or the medimnus (the measure); or how long will you go on measuring the dust? Ought you not to demonstrate those things which make men happy, which make things go on for them in the way as they wish, and why we ought to blame no man, accuse no man, and acquiesce in the administration of the universe?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want
